title: Literary Narrative: The Orchard Ledger
text:
My grandmother kept the orchard's ledger in a spiral notebook whose cover had gone soft as cloth from forty years of pockets. I had imagined, before I came to spend that autumn with her, that a ledger meant columns of money. Hers had almost no money in it. It had dates, and weather, and sentences.

April 9. Gravensteins in bloom, three days behind the Baldwins. Wind out of the north all week.

June 2. Row seven dropping fruit early. Row eight fine. Same rain, same sun, same everything.

I was sixteen and certain that the county extension office had already solved whatever my grandmother was trying to solve with a pencil. They published bulletins with graphs in them. They had degree-days and spray calendars and a phone number you could call. I told her this in the packing shed one morning while I sorted drops into the cider bin, and she did not argue. She said only that the bulletins were written for the county, and that she farmed eleven acres of it.

She had names for the trees, which embarrassed me in front of anyone who visited. The tall Northern Spy at the top of the hill was the Bishop. Two crooked Winesaps by the road were the Aunts. When I asked why she bothered, she said that a name was just a way of remembering that a thing was itself and not an average.

The frost came in the second week of May, later than any frost had a right to come. The radio said thirty-four degrees, which is not freezing, and every grower I knew of went to bed. My grandmother did not. She had me help her drag the smudge barrels out to the low ground at the eastern edge, where the land dished before it rose again, and we lit them at one in the morning and stood in the smoke until dawn like two people waiting for a train.

She had known because of the notebook. Cold air, she explained, behaves like water: it runs downhill and pools. Three times in forty years the low ground had frozen when the town had not, and each time she had written down the day, the wind, and the color of the evening sky beforehand. The pattern was not a law. It was a habit the land had, and she had learned it the way you learn a person's habits, by paying attention over a long time and writing it down so that you could not fool yourself later.

We lost the blossoms on the western slope, where we had not gone. The low ground held.

In October I asked if I could write an entry. She handed me the pencil without ceremony, the way you might hand someone a fork. I wrote the date, and the wind, and then I sat there for a long while, because I understood suddenly that the hard part was not the writing. The hard part was learning to see something worth writing down. Anyone can record a fact. It takes a season, at least, to notice one.

The Bishop gave nine bushels that year. I wrote that too, and underneath it, in my own handwriting, which looked wrong on the page: Row seven still dropping. Ask her why.

title: Literary Narrative: The Owl Route
text:
The 61 ran all night, and because it ran all night the transit authority called it an owl route, which was the first piece of local vocabulary I learned after moving to the city. I learned the rest of it on the bus.

I was twenty-two and working the overnight desk at a hotel that no longer exists. My shift ended at four in the morning, and the 61 came at 4:40, and there was nothing else to do with those forty minutes but stand under the shelter at Delacroix and Ninth and watch the traffic lights cycle through their colors for nobody.

The driver was named Marguerite. I know this because it was stenciled on a small placard she had made herself and taped beside the fare box, under the official one that said only OPERATOR 3312. She drove the owl four nights a week for eleven years, which meant she had watched a great many people become themselves at an hour when no one was performing.

There were maybe fifteen regulars. A man in a wool coat who read paperbacks with the covers torn off. Two sisters who cleaned offices downtown and argued the whole ride in a language I never identified. A woman named Ivy who worked the presses at a commercial laundry on Ashland and who was, without exception, late.

The schedule said the 61 left Ashland at 4:52. Ivy came out of the laundry door at 4:54, sometimes 4:55, walking fast and apologizing before she was close enough to be heard. And every night Marguerite sat at that stop with the door folded open and the engine idling, watching the mirror.

It bothered me for a while. I was young enough to think that a schedule was a kind of moral fact. One night in February, when the windows had gone opaque with our breath, I asked her about it.

"The paper says 4:52," she said. "Ivy says 4:54."

"But the schedule—"

"The schedule is a promise to the whole route," she said. "Waiting is a promise to Ivy. I've never once made the route late. I make up ninety seconds on Hollis where the lights are long, and forty on the viaduct, and the rest was never real to begin with, because whoever wrote that timetable has never driven it." She glanced at the mirror again. "Anyway. She has three stops after mine before she's home. If she misses me she misses all of it."

I rode the 61 for two years and four months. I have lived in four cities since, and I remember almost nothing about the streets of any of them, but I could still draw the owl route from memory: the long dark stretch past the rail yard, the church with the broken clock that said ten past two in every season, the place where the road lifted and for about six seconds you could see the whole grid of the city laid out and lit and mostly asleep.

Last spring a young man at a bus shelter asked me whether the night bus was reliable. I said yes. I said it comes when it says it comes, more or less, and then I heard myself add: and if you're running, run anyway. Somebody might be watching the mirror.

title: Literary Narrative: Proof
text:
The starter had a name. My great-grandmother had called it Ondine, and my father called it Ondine, and so at eleven I stood on a milk crate at the bench and called it Ondine too, and fed it flour and water at six in the evening as though it were a cat.

By the time I was twenty-four I had spent two years at a baking school in another city, where I had learned to speak about dough in numbers. Hydration percentage. Ambient temperature. Desired dough temperature, which you calculate by subtracting the flour temperature and the room temperature and the friction factor of your mixer from a number you have chosen in advance. I came home in June with a laminated conversion chart and a used proofing cabinet I had bought with my own money, a steel box with a digital controller that would hold the dough at any temperature I asked it to, to within half a degree.

My father looked at the cabinet the way you look at a relative's new spouse.

"It's a box," he said.

"It's a controlled environment."

"It's a box that costs money to be a room."

Our bakery had never had a controlled environment. It had a bench by the window that ran warm in the afternoon, a corner near the walk-in that ran cold, and a shelf above the oven that ran hot enough to be useless in July and perfect in February. My father moved the dough among these places the way a chess player moves pieces, and if you asked him how he knew, he would say the dough told him, which is the kind of answer that makes a person go to baking school.

The heat wave came in the third week of July. The shop hit ninety-four degrees before six in the morning. Every batch we mixed by the old method blew past its window while we were doing something else; the dough went slack and gassy and tore instead of stretching, and we sold flat, sour bread for two days to people too polite to say so. On the third morning my father, who had not looked at the cabinet since June, said, "Set your box to sixty-eight."

It worked. The dough came out of the cabinet exactly as it had come off the shelf in March, and I was insufferable about it for approximately four hours, until the second mix.

I had done everything the same. Same flour, same water, same sixty-eight degrees, same ninety minutes. My father walked past the tub, put two fingers into the dough without breaking stride, and said, "This one goes now."

"It has twenty minutes left."

"The flour's from the new pallet," he said. "It's thirstier. Twenty minutes and you'll be selling sour bread again."

He was right, and I have thought about why for years. The cabinet controlled the room. It could not know what had happened in a wheat field in another state, or that the sack had come off a truck that morning instead of sitting three weeks in our storeroom. It answered the question it had been built to answer, perfectly, forever.

We kept the cabinet. We also kept the shelf above the oven, and Ondine, and the habit of putting two fingers in.

I understand now that my father was not opposed to measurement. He was opposed to the idea that measurement could be finished.

title: Social Science: The Warm Half of the City
text:
On a still August evening, two thermometers a few miles apart in the same city can disagree by more than ten degrees. Neither is broken. The difference has a name that is now familiar to planners and increasingly familiar to residents: the urban heat island.

The physical mechanism is not mysterious. Dark asphalt and dark roofing absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them and release it slowly as heat through the night. Buildings and pavement store energy the way a brick oven does. Trees, by contrast, cool their surroundings twice over: they cast shade, and they move water from the soil into the air through their leaves, a process that consumes heat much as evaporating sweat does. A block with a closed canopy of mature street trees can run several degrees cooler at four in the afternoon than a treeless block of identical buildings.

What has surprised many people is not the physics but the map. When cities began measuring temperature at fine resolution, the pattern that emerged was not random. In city after city, the hottest neighborhoods were disproportionately those that had been marked as hazardous on federal lending maps in the 1930s, and the coolest were those marked as desirable. The correlation is not a claim that lending maps directly caused pavement to be laid. It reflects a long chain: neighborhoods denied investment received less park land, fewer street trees, more industrial zoning, and wider roads, and those decisions are still on the ground eighty years later. Tree canopy, it turns out, is one of the most durable records a city keeps of how it once distributed money.

Measuring the pattern took an unusual method. Fixed weather stations are sparse and are often sited at airports, which are flat, open, and unrepresentative. To get street-level data, researchers in dozens of cities have recruited volunteers to drive fixed routes on a single hot day, carrying sensors mounted on car windows, sampling at one-second intervals in the morning, afternoon, and evening. The resulting maps are detailed enough to show a cool ribbon along a creek and a hot plateau over a shopping center parking lot.

Knowing where the heat is does not by itself say what to do about it. Reflective roof coatings are cheap and work immediately, but they cool the building beneath more than the sidewalk beside it. Shade trees do cool the street, but they take fifteen to twenty-five years to reach useful size, and a tree planted without a maintenance budget is likely to die within three summers. Meanwhile, residents of the neighborhoods with the least canopy do not always greet planting campaigns warmly. Some object to the leaf litter and sidewalk damage they will be expected to manage themselves; others have watched greening projects in nearby districts precede rising rents, and reasonably ask whether the shade will still be theirs when it arrives.

The most careful programs have responded by treating heat as a problem of both material and tenure. They pair planting with multi-year watering contracts, hire from the neighborhoods being planted, and combine slow canopy work with fast measures that help this summer: cooled bus shelters, extended library hours, and rules limiting utility shutoffs during heat emergencies. That combination is less photogenic than a row of saplings. It reflects an unglamorous finding of the research: heat kills on specific afternoons, and a tree that will be tall in 2045 is no help in the meantime.

title: Social Science: The Invention of the Public Park
text:
It is easy to assume that public parks are as old as cities. They are not. For most of urban history, open ground inside a town was either private, agricultural, or sacred: a nobleman's hunting preserve, a common where households with rights could graze animals, a churchyard. The idea that a municipality should buy land, plant it, and keep it permanently open to anyone who walked in is a nineteenth-century invention, and it had to be argued for.

The argument was made in the language of the day, which was the language of disease, morality, and property. Reformers in industrial cities pointed to overcrowded districts where families lived several to a room and argued that open ground was a sanitary necessity, calling parks the lungs of the city. That phrase was more than metaphor to its users; before the germ theory of disease was widely accepted, many physicians attributed epidemics to foul air rising from crowded ground, and a park was understood as ventilation. Others argued in moral terms, claiming that workers with somewhere pleasant to spend Sunday would spend less of it drinking. A third argument, and the one that most often persuaded councils, was financial: land facing a new park would rise in value, and the taxes on it would repay the purchase.

The first parks reflected this mixed parentage. Designed landscapes of the mid-century typically offered curving paths, artificial lakes, and carefully framed views of meadow and grove, arranged so that a visitor would experience a sequence of scenes rather than a single vista. Designers spoke of the restorative effect of such scenery on people worn down by streets and machinery. The parks were also, in many cases, rule-bound places. Keeping off the grass, restrictions on ball games, bans on public speaking, and closing hours were common, and they reveal that the park was intended for a particular kind of use: strolling, looking, and being seen behaving well. Working-class visitors who wanted a field for football rather than a lawn for promenading had to campaign, sometimes for decades, to change these rules.

The property argument, meanwhile, contained a difficulty that would outlast the century. If a park raises the value of the land around it, then the park makes the neighborhood beside it more expensive, and the households most in need of open ground may be the least able to remain next to it. Nineteenth-century advocates generally treated the rise in value as pure benefit. Contemporary planners are more likely to treat it as a design constraint, coupling new open space with commitments about housing.

The park idea also kept changing shape. Large landscape parks were followed by small neighborhood playgrounds, then by playing fields, then, more recently, by projects far more modest in scale: converted rail lines, plazas made by closing a block to cars, and vacant lots cleaned, seeded, and given a low fence. Studies of these smallest interventions have reported measurable effects, including reductions in residents' reported stress and in certain kinds of crime on the surrounding blocks, though researchers caution that such findings are difficult to separate from other changes happening at the same time.

What survives from the original argument is the least measurable part of it. Whatever else a park is, it is a piece of a city that a person may enter without paying, buying, belonging, or explaining why. In a dense place, that turns out to be an unusual thing to own in common.

title: Social Science: What the Trash Knows
text:
People are unreliable narrators of their own habits. This is not usually dishonesty. Ask a household how much food it threw away last week and the answer will be shaped by memory, by embarrassment, and by an honest inability to recall a wilted bag of greens. For decades, nearly everything social scientists knew about consumption came from asking. Then a small number of researchers decided to look instead at what people had already thrown out.

The discipline that resulted is sometimes called garbology. Its founding insight was borrowed from archaeology, which has always drawn its conclusions from refuse rather than from testimony; a midden of shells and broken pottery tells you what a settlement actually ate and used, without the flattering edits of a chronicle. The innovation was to apply the method to living communities. Beginning in the early 1970s, one long-running university project sorted, weighed, and catalogued household waste collected from sampled neighborhoods, recording every item by material, brand, and quantity.

The results repeatedly contradicted the surveys. Households consistently reported drinking less alcohol than their discarded containers indicated and eating more fresh produce than their waste stream confirmed. Reported and measured food waste diverged sharply, with actual discards running well above what people believed they threw out. One of the most counterintuitive findings concerned scarcity: when a shortage or a price spike made a staple item newsworthy, waste of that item tended to rise rather than fall, because households bought unfamiliar substitutes and unusual quantities and then failed to use them.

A second line of work turned from fresh curbside waste to landfills, where crews extracted core samples from buried decades. The prevailing public image of a landfill was a compost heap in which organic matter quietly returned to soil. Excavations found something closer to a sealed archive. Deprived of oxygen and moisture, materials decomposed far more slowly than expected; newspapers pulled from strata forty years deep were often legible enough to read the date and, incidentally, to date the layer around them. Buried food waste was frequently identifiable by type. The practical implication was uncomfortable for waste policy, because it meant that the volume problem in landfills was driven less by food and yard debris than by paper, packaging, and construction debris that would persist essentially unchanged.

The method has real limits, and its practitioners have generally been candid about them. Garbage is anonymous by design in these studies; records are aggregated to the level of a route or a census tract, never a household, both for ethics and because a single week's bin is a poor sample. Waste can only report what is discarded, so items that are given away, repaired, composted at home, or hoarded in a garage are invisible to it. Recycling diverts an increasing share of the record. And the method describes without explaining: it can establish that a neighborhood discarded a great deal of a particular product, but not why.

Even so, the basic contribution is durable, and it is methodological rather than topical. Where self-report and material evidence disagree, the disagreement is itself data. It maps the distance between how people understand their own behavior and what their behavior leaves behind, and that gap is often the most useful thing a study of consumption can measure.

title: Humanities: The Restorer's Hand
text:
A conservator I once watched at work described her job in a way that startled me. She said she was not repairing the painting. She was arguing with the future.

The painting in front of her was a small fifteenth-century panel of an almond harvest, and it had a problem common to panels of its age: the wooden support had shrunk across the grain over five centuries while the paint layer had not, and the result was a network of cracks and, in three places, losses where flakes of paint had fallen away entirely, leaving bare gesso the color of a fingernail.

What should be done about a loss is the oldest argument in the field, and it is not a technical question. Fill it and paint it so convincingly that no visitor can find it, and you have given the public an experience close to the artist's intention, at the cost of putting your own invention where his brushwork used to be. Leave it blank, and you have been scrupulously honest at the cost of a hole in the middle of a face. Neither choice is neutral. Both are interpretations, and both will be inherited by people who did not consent to them.

The profession's answer has been a set of principles rather than a formula. The first is reversibility: whatever the conservator adds should be removable by a future colleague without harming what lies beneath, which is why fills are made with materials deliberately weaker than the original and retouching is done in resins chosen because they can be dissolved again. The second is that intervention should be confined to the loss and never extended over surviving original paint. The third, and the most philosophically interesting, is that the addition should be detectable on inspection even when it is invisible at a normal viewing distance. One well-known technique achieves this with fine parallel strokes of pure color that fuse into the surrounding tone when you step back, but resolve into obvious hatching when you lean in. A visitor sees a whole picture. A specialist with a raking light sees exactly where the twenty-first century begins.

These principles were hard won, largely through public quarrels. The cleaning controversies of the mid-twentieth century, in which museums removed centuries of darkened varnish and were accused of stripping paintings of their intended atmosphere, forced the field to articulate what it had previously done by instinct. Critics argued that the brownish tone of an old master was part of how the work had been experienced for generations and had acquired a legitimacy of its own. Conservators replied that varnish is not the artist's work, that it yellows unevenly, and that the accumulated gloom was an accident being mistaken for a style. The dispute never fully resolved, but it produced a habit that now defines the discipline: document everything, publish the reasoning, and assume that your successors will disagree with you.

That assumption explains the conservator's remark. The most consequential decisions in her field are made not about the object as it is but about the object as it will be handled by people not yet born, working with instruments not yet invented, holding opinions she cannot predict. She could not make the panel young again; nobody can. What she could do was slow its decay, refuse to disguise her own hand, and leave the next conservator more choices than she had been left herself. Restraint, in that light, is not modesty. It is a form of generosity extended forward in time.

title: Humanities: Hands That Rhyme
text:
The most persistent misunderstanding about sign languages is that they are not languages at all, but rather a system of gestures standing in for the words of a spoken language. A related misunderstanding is that there is one of them, used everywhere. Both ideas collapse on contact with evidence. American Sign Language and British Sign Language are mutually unintelligible, despite the shared spoken language of their surrounding hearing communities, and neither maps onto English word order or English grammar.

Linguists established the point by treating signs the way phonologists treat spoken words: as combinations of smaller contrastive units. A sign can be analyzed into a handshape, a location on or near the body, a movement, and an orientation of the palm, along with non-manual markers carried by the face and posture. Change only one of these and the meaning changes, exactly as swapping one sound in a spoken word produces another word. Pairs of signs that differ in a single parameter function as minimal pairs, the classic evidence that a system has structure below the level of the word.

Grammar lives partly in space. A signer can establish a person or thing at a point in the space in front of the body and then refer back to that point, so that spatial arrangement does the work that pronouns and case endings do elsewhere. Verbs can be directed between established points to show who acts on whom. Non-manual markers are grammatical rather than merely expressive: a particular configuration of the brows, held across a phrase, can mark it as a question or a conditional clause, and dropping it makes the sentence ungrammatical rather than simply flat.

Because these languages use hands, face, and space simultaneously, they can express in one moment what a spoken sentence must lay out in sequence. This has consequences for poetry. Where a spoken poem may rhyme by repeating sounds at the ends of lines, a signed poem can rhyme by repeating a handshape across successive signs, so that a passage is unified by, say, a single closed fist recurring in different locations. Poets exploit symmetry between the two hands, balance and tension in the body, and transitions in which one sign melts into the next without a neutral rest. A line break may be marked by a hold. Because two hands can sign different things at once, a poet can present two images simultaneously and let the viewer see the comparison rather than hear it stated.

None of this survives translation intact. Rendering a signed poem into written English converts a simultaneous art into a sequential one, and the result reads as a paraphrase of something that happened rather than the thing itself. Video changed the field decisively for this reason: before recording, a signed poem existed only in performance and memory, and a tradition could be lost within a generation.

That fragility was not accidental. For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, educational policy in many countries suppressed signing in favor of speech and lipreading, and children were punished for using their hands. The languages survived anyway, transmitted in dormitories, playgrounds, clubs, and families, which is to say by communities rather than institutions. Linguists arriving later to describe these languages were documenting something that had been preserved in spite of formal education, not because of it.

The modern consensus is unremarkable as science and remarkable as history: these are full natural languages, with dialects, registers, slang, historical change, and literature, acquired by children on an ordinary timetable when they are exposed to them early enough.

title: Humanities: The Long Life of a Typeface
text:
Almost no one notices type, which is the point. A typeface that draws attention to itself in a novel has failed at the only job it was hired to do. And yet the shapes on the page are designed objects with histories, arguments, and consequences, and the people who make them have been quarreling about the same questions for five hundred years.

The first of those questions is whether letters should imitate writing or resist it. Early European printers cut their type in imitation of the manuscript hands their customers already read, because a book that looked unfamiliar looked untrustworthy. Later designers pulled steadily away from the pen: strokes became more even, the contrast between thick and thin grew sharper, and the diagonal stress inherited from a slanted nib rotated upright. By the late eighteenth century some faces had been engineered into pure geometry, admired for their crispness and criticized for a glittering, brittle quality on the page. Each generation described its own preference as clarity and its predecessors' as either crudeness or decoration.

The second question is what legibility actually is, and whether it can be measured. Nineteenth-century arguments were largely aesthetic. In the twentieth century researchers began testing reading speed, error rates, and recognition at distance, and the results were less decisive than either side had hoped. Under ordinary conditions, competent text faces perform similarly; readers are fast with what they read often. This raised an uncomfortable possibility: that much of what we call legibility is familiarity, and that a face feels readable because we have read it, not the other way around.

The exception is extreme conditions, and this is where the research earned its keep. Signage read at speed by a driver, labels on medication, instruments glanced at rather than studied: here differences between designs are measurable and sometimes large. Designers of road-sign alphabets found that letters must be distinguished at low resolution and from far away, which favors open apertures, generous spacing, and shapes that stay distinct when blurred. A lowercase l, a capital I, and the digit 1 that converge into one form at a distance are a safety problem, not a matter of taste. Faces designed for such use are often unremarkable up close and unmistakable at four hundred feet.

The third question is whether a typeface can carry meaning independent of the words it sets. Designers generally say yes and historians agree, because forms acquire associations by use: a face used for decades on official documents comes to look official, and one used on wartime posters carries that history into any later setting. This is not intrinsic to the shapes. It is accumulated, and it can fade. A face that struck readers as aggressively modern in its own decade may read as quaint in the next, unchanged in every measurement and transformed in effect.

Which is why revivals are so difficult. To reissue a face cut in the sixteenth century, a designer must decide what was intended and what was accident: the irregularities of hand-cut punches, the way ink spread into damp paper and softened every corner, the fact that each size was cut separately and was never meant to be scaled. A digital revival that reproduces the drawing exactly will look thin and mechanical, because it has removed the ink. Faithfulness turns out to require deliberate departure, and the reviver, like the conservator, is making an argument about the past in a medium that cannot show its own reasoning.

title: Natural Science: Dialects in the Dawn Chorus
text:
Drive an hour along a coastal range in early spring and stop twice, and the sparrows singing at the two stops may not sound the same. The species is identical. The songs are not. They share an overall architecture, a whistle followed by a buzz and a trill, but the details of pitch, the number of trill notes, and the ordering of the parts differ consistently from one valley to the next. Birds within a valley sound like each other. Birds a few miles away sound like each other in a different way. Biologists call these regional variants dialects, and the analogy is more than loose, because the mechanism behind them is the same one behind human dialects: learning.

A young sparrow is not born knowing its song. It hatches with an innate template general enough to identify its own species and to rule out the songs of others, but the specific version it will sing must be acquired by listening to adults during a sensitive period early in life. It then passes through a stage of subsong, a rambling and variable practice phase, and gradually crystallizes a stable adult version that it will keep. Birds raised in isolation produce abnormal, simplified songs. Birds tutored with recordings sing what they were played, provided the recordings are of their own species and arrive during the sensitive window.

Because the song is copied, it is subject to the ordinary consequences of copying. Errors occur and are sometimes reproduced by the next generation. Local versions drift. When investigators have compared archival recordings from the same locations across several decades, they have found that dialect boundaries move, that some variants spread while others vanish, and that occasional new elements appear and are then imitated. Song is thus culturally transmitted, and it evolves on a timescale much faster than the birds' genes do.

The obvious question is whether dialects matter to the birds themselves. Playback experiments provide part of the answer: territorial males typically respond more strongly to a local dialect than to a foreign one, approaching the speaker and answering more often, which suggests they treat an unfamiliar dialect as a less immediate threat. Females of some species show preferences in laboratory tests for the dialect of the area where they were reared. Whether that adds up to reduced interbreeding between dialect regions is disputed, and studies using genetic markers have generally found less separation than the acoustic differences might suggest. Birds move, and a bird that settles in a new valley may modify its song toward the local version.

Human noise has become a variable of its own. Traffic and machinery produce sound concentrated at low frequencies, and birds in noisy areas have been recorded singing at higher minimum frequencies, more loudly, and sometimes at different hours, shifting toward dawn or into the night when the roads are quieter. Some of these adjustments happen within an individual's lifetime; others appear to be learned changes passed between generations. The adjustments are not free. Raising a song's pitch can reduce the traits that make it attractive, and a bird that is heard may nonetheless be judged less impressive.

The wider significance is that a behavior essential to reproduction is transmitted by learning rather than fixed by inheritance. That makes it flexible, which is an advantage in a changing acoustic world. It also makes it fragile: a tradition maintained by imitation can be lost in a few generations if the population thins and there are too few singers left for the young to hear.

title: Natural Science: The Water Under the Desert
text:
A visitor to a desert basin will notice the dry riverbeds first. They are wide, pale, floored with sand and rounded gravel, and they carry no water at all for most of the year. They look like the ruins of a wetter climate. In fact they are working parts of a living system, and most of the water in the basin passes through them, briefly and violently, a few times a decade.

Desert hydrology is dominated by rare events. In a temperate watershed, the annual average rainfall is a reasonable guide to how much water moves through the landscape. In an arid one, the average is nearly useless, because most of the small storms that make up the average evaporate or are taken up by shallow-rooted plants before they penetrate more than a few inches of soil. What matters is the exceptional storm: an intense downpour that exceeds the soil's ability to absorb it and generates runoff. A channel may run once in three years and, in those hours, carry more water than the preceding thousand days combined. Flash floods often arrive under a clear sky, because the storm that produced them fell on high ground far upstream.

Where that flood goes is the central question. Some of it evaporates; some reaches a playa and stands in a shallow sheet until the sun removes it. But a large fraction soaks downward through the coarse sand and gravel of the channel bed, a process hydrologists call transmission loss, which is a misleading name from the perspective of the aquifer, since the water is not lost but delivered. Coarse channel sediments are the most permeable material in the basin, and the streambed acts as a long, narrow funnel into the alluvial aquifer beneath. Recharge in such basins is therefore concentrated in space as well as in time: it happens along channels, during floods.

How much reaches the deeper groundwater can be estimated by dating it. Water carries chemical signatures, including isotopes whose ratios reflect the temperature at which precipitation formed and radioactive constituents that decay at known rates. In many desert basins, deep groundwater dates to the late Pleistocene, when the regional climate was cooler and wetter. That water is essentially a nonrenewable deposit. Where wells draw from such reserves faster than modern recharge replaces them, the activity is closer to mining than to harvesting, and the arithmetic is not ambiguous: aquifers with recharge measured in millimeters per year cannot indefinitely support withdrawals measured in centimeters.

Vegetation complicates the accounting in an instructive way. Along a channel with shallow groundwater, deep-rooted trees and shrubs known as phreatophytes tap the water table directly and return substantial quantities to the atmosphere. Removing them increases the water available for wells, which was once proposed as a management strategy. It also removes the shade and root structure that hold the channel banks in place and shelter most of the basin's wildlife, and the practice is now generally regarded as a poor bargain.

Recent management has tried to work with the natural pattern rather than against it. Managed recharge diverts floodwater into shallow spreading basins where it can infiltrate over days instead of hours, and check structures slow flows so that more water enters the bed. These methods do not create water. They capture more of what already arrives, which in a desert is the only kind of gain available.

title: Natural Science: The Gift of the Ash
text:
One of the more stubborn puzzles of human settlement is that people live on the slopes of active volcanoes. They know the risk; they usually have direct family memory of it. They stay, and they plant, and the reason is in the soil.

Volcanic ash begins as molten rock that is torn apart and quenched so rapidly that its atoms have no time to organize into crystals. The result is a glass, and glass of this kind is chemically unstable at the earth's surface. It weathers quickly, releasing calcium, magnesium, potassium, and phosphorus at rates that ordinary rock cannot match. Soils formed on volcanic ash therefore acquire, within centuries rather than the millennia typical elsewhere, a mineral wealth that farmers can exploit.

Their physical structure is equally unusual. Weathering ash produces minerals with an enormous internal surface area and a fluffy, low-density texture. Such soils hold two or three times more water than a comparable sandy soil while remaining loose enough that roots and air move through them easily. They resist compaction, drain well after heavy rain, and stay moist through short droughts. Farmers describe them as forgiving, and the description is accurate: they tolerate both too much water and too little better than most soils do.

The picture is not uniformly favorable. The same reactive minerals that make these soils fertile also bind phosphorus tightly, holding it in forms plants cannot take up, so growers may need to apply far more phosphate fertilizer than the soil's total phosphorus content would suggest. The soils are also light, and on steep slopes stripped of vegetation they erode readily.

The fertility takes time to arrive, and the sequence is worth following. Fresh ash immediately after an eruption is not soil. It is sterile, unstructured mineral matter with no organic content and no capacity to hold nutrients in place, and in the first years after a major fall, crops planted in it typically fail. Colonization begins with organisms that need almost nothing: lichens and mosses that etch the glass surfaces, then plants able to fix atmospheric nitrogen, since nitrogen is the one major nutrient ash does not supply. As these die and decompose, organic matter accumulates and binds the mineral particles, and the ash becomes a soil. Depending on rainfall, temperature, and the grain size of the deposit, useful agricultural fertility may appear within a decade or take a century.

For geologists, the same deposits have a second value. A large eruption spreads ash across a wide area within days, and that layer, once buried, is a chronological marker of unusual precision: everything below it is older, everything above it is younger, and its chemistry can identify which eruption produced it. Correlating tephra layers between distant sites allows lake sediments, ice, peat bogs, and archaeological deposits to be tied to a single timeline. A layer of ash in a farmer's field and the same layer in a bog forty miles away record the same afternoon.

So the volcano gives twice, and both gifts are entangled with the hazard. The eruption that buries a village replenishes the ground that fed it, on a schedule measured in generations rather than seasons. The settlements are not evidence that people misjudge the danger. They are evidence of a bargain in which the same event supplies both terms.
